abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.

sections.body: User embeddings are dense vectors that encode user behavior for recommendation and personalization, but they are not interpretable and cannot be queried in natural language. The paper applies the superposition hypothesis from mechanistic interpretability, arguing that user embeddings encode behavioral modes in superposition. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can recover these modes, and auto-interpretation can name them. The method is post-hoc: it needs only pre-trained embeddings, discovers modes without labels, and gives graded mode assignments. The authors compare it with predefined taxonomies and per-user LLM labeling, which need raw interaction data. They describe per-user LLM labeling as prohibitively expensive at scale. Validation uses synthetic data with known modes and two public datasets.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: User embeddings are opaque, and the paper argues they decompose into sparse, named behavioral modes.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into four areas. Sparse autoencoders have been applied to language model activations and to text, image, audio, and other embeddings, but these methods ground latents in the semantics of the input modality, not in behavior. Two concurrent recommender studies insert sparse autoencoders into collaborative filtering or sequential recommenders, targeting steering or control rather than decomposition of pre-trained user embeddings. Critiques report that sparse autoencoders can fail to recover ground-truth features and that frozen-random decoders can match trained ones at high overcompleteness. Disentangled recommenders need training-time objectives, and topic models operate on raw interactions. Lookalike audience modeling requires seed users and gives no view of the behavioral drivers.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior sparse autoencoder work covers text and non-text embeddings and two recommender settings, but not post-hoc behavioral decomposition.

sections.body: The section models each user as a mixture: every interaction comes from one of K behavioral modes, weighted by user-specific non-negative weights that sum to one and form a sparse subset. When the embedding is a sample mean of per-observation features, the embedding equals a sparse weighted sum of mode centroids in expectation, $\mathbf{u}\approx\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\,\mathbf{d}_{k}$. Centroids can be correlated, so the method needs overcomplete dictionaries rather than orthogonal ones such as principal components. For transformer encoders the claim rests on the superposition hypothesis and is tested empirically. The argument does not directly cover single-position readouts or attention-driven context effects, which may produce finer latents. Under the flat model, extra splits of one mode are artifacts that can be merged post-hoc.
sections.heading: Superposition from a generative model of user behavior
sections.headline: A mixed-membership generative model implies user embeddings are sparse linear combinations of mode centroids in expectation.

sections.body: The section tests mode recovery on synthetic data with known ground truth: 100,000 users, K=75 modes, and mean-pooled product embeddings projected to m from 16 to 128. The sparse autoencoder has `d_hidden`=300, with a sparsity penalty matched to the ground-truth mean number of modes per user. Against random projections, sparsified PCA and FastICA, K-Means encoding, and NMF, it matches or exceeds every classical baseline when m is below 75. K-Means holds near 80% recovery, while PCA recovers at most 9% of modes. Merging features with decoder cosine above 0.45 raises median per-feature correlation from approximately 0.35 to approximately 0.70 at m=128. On a trained SASRec encoder, the sparse autoencoder reaches code-GT alignment 0.58 and recovers 73 of 75 modes. The authors note that nonlinear encoders satisfy the structure only approximately.
sections.heading: Experiments on Synthetic Data
sections.headline: On synthetic data with known modes, the sparse autoencoder matches or exceeds classical baselines in the overcomplete regime below 75 dimensions.

sections.body: The section evaluates on Open e-commerce (1.8M purchases from 5027 consumers, with life-event survey labels) and MovieLens 1M. An LLM names each sparse autoencoder latent from its top-activating users. At query time, an LLM scores each feature's relevance from 0 to 10, keeps features scoring at least 5, and ranks users by a weighted sum of their activations. On Open e-commerce, SAE Lift is 1.93× on category tasks versus 1.86× for FastICA, and 5.30× versus 4.75× on life-event tasks. SAE FVU is 0.075 versus 0.083 for FastICA, but FastICA has higher Coverage. On MovieLens, SAE Lift is 2.53 versus 2.16 for K-Means encoding on SASRec, but 2.38 versus 2.41 on BERT4Rec. The MovieLens gain is mainly in coverage: 0.977 versus 0.811 on SASRec.
sections.heading: Behavioral Modes in Real World Data
sections.headline: On Open e-commerce, sparse autoencoder retrieval matches or exceeds every classical sparse baseline on every retrieval-quality metric.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the framework: classical and transformer user embeddings decompose into sparse superpositions of behavioral modes that sparse autoencoders can recover. On synthetic data, they recover more known modes than classical methods, including for transformer-encoded embeddings. The authors name several limits: they tested only ReLU sparse autoencoders, only positive-only consumption domains, and only transformer sequential recommenders, and they considered at most two temporal snapshots per user. The weighted-sum combinator cannot express logical constraints or temporal sequencing. On privacy, they state that natural-language querying lowers the cost of inferring sensitive traits such as recent life events. They add that named, enumerable features allow sensitive directions to be detected, excluded, or ablated, which dense embeddings do not allow.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The method enables natural-language audience retrieval over embeddings never trained on text, and the authors flag privacy risk.

sections.body: This appendix gives details for the synthetic experiments. Claude Opus 4.6 defined 75 modes across five domains, and Claude Sonnet 4 wrote purchase histories for 100,000 users, with 99,832 parsed successfully and 5,803,030 interactions. Table 3 compares item popularity: the synthetic data places 50.9% of interactions on its top 1% of items, against 19.1% for Open e-commerce and 8.7% for MovieLens 1M. Tables 4 and 5 list all 75 modes. The appendix also covers SAE and baseline settings, mode recovery at cosine thresholds from 0.5 to 0.8, the soft-frozen decoder check, SASRec trained on synthetic sequences, engagement-axis relabeling for MovieLens, and the LLM prompts used for interpretation, scoring, and behavioral summaries.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the synthetic setup, the 75 mode taxonomy, baseline details, cosine-threshold and soft-frozen-decoder checks, transformer embeddings, and prompts.
